detail.text: Sluter is one of the very few sculptors of the period whose name survives attached to work, and he is credited with introducing an unprecedented realism into European sculpture around 1400. The evidence is in the drapery here: Mary's cloak and John's robe hang and fold as cloth actually hangs, which is not how carving had been done.

The cross is carved as a truncated living trunk, rooted in a rocky ground, with a dead sawn branch halfway up where an angel hovers. Underneath the roots is a hollow, and in it a lioness tends her cubs — an old symbol of the resurrection, tucked where you have to crouch to find it.

Jacob Appel painted the house in 1710, and that painting hangs in this same room; the rooms have changed remarkably little since he recorded them. What is missing is the people: the original dolls are gone. The state bought the house in 1821 and the Rijksmuseum acquired it in 1875.

detail.text: Nothing is known about the vessel or about who made the model. Those three are what the museum's catalogue puts its conclusion on.

The rest is a shipwright's document. Gun ports along two decks with every gun missing; a crowned lion as figurehead; a glass dome over the quarterdeck to light the cabin below; a six-oared launch hanging from davits at the stern; a steering wheel against the mizzen mast. The stern also carries the monogram LAL under a crown.

The work was divided the way a real ship's would be. Adriaen de Vriend and Adriaen Davidsen made the model in Flushing, Cornelis Moerman did the carving, and Cornelis Evertsen II oversaw the rigging. No actual vessel matches it exactly, although it may loosely stand for the 94-gun Koning William.

detail.text: It is a group portrait as much as a battle. Pieneman spent nearly four months in London in 1821, working from a studio Wellington let him set up in Apsley House; the duke sat for him, arranged sittings with other commanders, and had Copenhagen brought over to be painted from life. The finished canvas took almost three years.

Wellington may have meant to buy it. Instead the Prince of Orange did, for 40,000 guilders, a sum his father William I actually paid. Pieneman made it a condition of the sale that he could show the painting in London first: a pavilion was built for it in Hyde Park, and it drew crowds there for some ten months from May 1825, including the tenth anniversary of the battle.

Lying wounded on a stretcher at the lower left is the Dutch Prince of Orange, later King William II — which is the reason a Dutch museum owns the picture at all.

Bosch's followers copied it again and again. Like the versions in Berlin and Philadelphia, this one keeps only the central scene, with no wings and no arched top with a landscape.

Hals was in Amsterdam at the time trying to finish the Meagre Company, whose sitters had refused to make the same journey; this couple went instead, and got the portraits.

For well over a century the pair carried the wrong names. The museum's first director attached them in 1885 to a different Amsterdam couple; the wills of that couple's heirs show the pictures cannot have passed down that line, and comparison with two later portraits of Van de Poll — as a militia colonel, painted by other hands — settled who this is.

detail.text: This is the high point of Hals's rough manner: loose strokes laid in varying thicknesses, sometimes shaped with the wrong end of the brush, reading as speed close up and as movement from across the room. Painters who work this way have no way back — nothing here is corrected or glazed over.

Whether it is a portrait at all is disputed. The man shows his teeth, and polite company of the 1620s did not laugh with its mouth open, which argues for a genre figure rather than a sitter. Nobody has identified him. The museum bought the painting in 1816, and a restoration in 1971 took off a discoloured varnish that had been flattening Hals's colours.

He was an Antwerp painter, and his market and kitchen pieces fed into the whole later development of still life in northern Europe.

detail.text: The props carry the argument. A cittern in Dutch painting of the period stands for love, often the carnal sort; the slipper kicked off in the foreground says much the same thing; the broom and the chair left in the doorway say that the housework has been set down mid-task. Above the seascape hangs a landscape with a traveller on a sandy road, which is usually read as the absent man who wrote the letter.

In 1971 the painting was stolen from a loan exhibition in Brussels. The thief hid in a cupboard until closing time, found the frame would not fit through the window, cut the canvas out with a potato peeler and eventually kept it in his pillowcase. His demand was 200 million Belgian francs for famine relief in East Pakistan. It came back eight days later, badly damaged, and took almost a year to restore.

kids: She has just been given a letter. What do you think it says?

look.text: The doorway and the drawn-back curtain, which make you an eavesdropper.
The seascape and the landscape on the back wall.
The slippers, the broom and the chair, left where they fell.

timeline.text: You are in the dark, looking through an open doorway into a lit room, past a curtain that has been pulled aside. A maid has just handed her mistress a letter; the woman has a cittern in her lap and has looked up from it. Everything about the framing says that you are not supposed to be seeing this.

closer: The patient is tied to his chair. Around the round central scene, sketchy grotesque figures crowd the edge.

detail.text: The scene is based on what may be Bosch's own painting of the subject, now in Madrid, inscribed "Meester snijt de keye ras, Mijne name is lubbert das". That reads "Master, cut the stone out quickly. My name is Lubbert Das". The name Lubbert Das means Doltish Ninny, which is the joke: the man asking to be cured of folly is called a fool.

The museum dates this panel to around 1550-1600 and attributes it to the manner of Bosch. Onlookers sit at a table on the right, and a stone already cut from someone's head lies on the table before them.

displayTitle: Removing the Rocks in the Head
kids: What do you think the surgeon is really cutting out of his head?

look.text: The patient, tied into the chair while the surgeon works on his head.
The onlookers at the table, with a cut stone laid out.
The grotesque figures sketched around the edge.

timeline.text: A surgeon cuts a stone out of a patient's head, a folk cure for foolishness that the picture treats as a joke on the fool who believes it.

closer: The wood tells part of the story. Three oak planks make the support, and tree-ring dating says the youngest ring grew in 1569, so the panel was probably painted no earlier than about 1594.

detail.text: A little man playing the bagpipes is carried out of the kitchen on a table, and his pitcher of drink has fallen over. Around the fireplace the work is all Shrove Tuesday, and the cleaning of fish points to Lent. A woman carries a round table on her head with just two fish on it, the meagre Lenten diet.

In the foreground two couples, monks and nuns, dance the dance of fools. An inscription reads "Dit is den dans van Luther met zijn nonne": this is the dance of Luther with his nun. The museum's own curators doubt the work is even after Bosch. Only the musicians inside the giant bagpipe recall him, and they suggest the composition was invented in Antwerp around 1560.

kids: Count how many people are eating and how many are dancing. Which side is winning?

look.text: The bagpiper carried out of the kitchen on the left.
The dancing monks and nuns in the foreground.
The giant bagpipe on the right, with a lute-player inside.

timeline.text: A crowded street scene, nearly two and a half metres wide, pits Carnival against Lent: feasting against fasting, excess against moderation.

closer: He signed it as graffiti. Look on the wall of the wooden shed for the ligatured letters ‘HAenricus / Av’.

detail.text: The picture owes a great deal to Pieter Bruegel the Elder's Winter Landscape with a Bird Trap of 1565, and the bird trap itself reappears here at the left, among the farm implements. Avercamp used the motif in other paintings too.

Nothing has been prettified. A dog is at a carcass in the lower left corner, and in the foreground a group of men are working to free a boat frozen into the ice. The museum bought the panel in 1897 with the support of the Vereniging Rembrandt.

dimensions.display: support: height 77.3 cm x width 131.9 cm

kids: Find someone who has fallen over. Now find three more.

look.text: The signature scratched into the wall of the shed.
Rich and poor on the same ice, at the same size.
The dog and the carcass at the lower left, which nobody has tidied away.

timeline.text: A whole society on one frozen river, seen from high up so that nobody outranks anybody else: skaters, kolf players, people out walking, a horse-drawn sleigh at the right, a church at the left. Avercamp painted it around 1608, after the bitter winter of 1607–08, and was the first Dutch painter to make snow his speciality.

closer: Nothing in this picture could have met anything else in it. That is the point of a menagerie, and the point of an empire.

detail.text: A royal menagerie was a collection in the same sense as a cabinet of curiosities: living proof of how far the ships went. Hondecoeter specialised in painting them, and he paints each bird as an individual — plumage, posture, eye — rather than as a decorative motif, which is why the picture still works as a picture and not only as an inventory.

The signature is under the vase. The balustrade, the oriental carpet thrown over it and the dark oak at the right are all stage furniture; the animals are the subject, and there are more of them than a first look finds.

name.en: King Stadtholder William III and Mary Stuart / Delftware
name.nl: Koning-stadhouder Willem III en Mary Stuart / Delfts aardewerk

kids: Count the birds. Then count the ones that are looking at you.

look.text: The white cockatoo on the rim of the vase, crest half up.
The two monkeys on the carpet at the right — the only mammals in the picture.
The gold chain, which is what all this beauty was actually attached to.

timeline.text: Cockatoos from Australia, a grey parrot from Africa, a lory from Indonesia, squirrel monkeys from Central America — all arranged on a garden balustrade around a stone vase. The painting hung over the door of William III's private apartment at Het Loo.

closer: The white dress is not white. Come close enough to see the pink and the blue-grey he used to keep it alive.

detail.text: She is dressed as a small adult, which is what seventeenth-century children were dressed as; her parents, the cloth merchant Gerard van der Schalcke and Johanna Bardoel, were painted by Ter Borch too. The carnation in her hand is a standard motif in portraits of the period, read as resurrection and the hope of eternal life.
That reading is worth holding onto. Helena died in 1671, at twenty-five, and the picture of her at two is the one that survived.

kids: She is two years old. Do you think she wanted to stand still for this?

look.text: The dress: white built out of pink and blue-grey.
The wicker basket, sized for a two-year-old.
The carnation, held out towards you.

timeline.text: Helena van der Schalcke was two years old when Ter Borch painted her, standing full length in white silk with a wicker basket over her arm and a carnation in her hand. The panel is about the size of a sheet of paper.

closer: This panel was once the middle section of a triptych. It repeats the central group of figures from Bosch's Temptation of St Anthony in Lisbon.

detail.text: Bosch painted the Lisbon triptych around 1500-1510, and it was copied many times. The best copy, a signed one now in Brussels, is the earliest, from around 1520-1530. This one belongs to that long line of copies.
A burning city glows in the background. A city on fire is the traditional sign of Anthony's protection against ergotism, the burning sickness his monks treated, also called Saint Anthony's fire.

dimensions.display: frame: height 89 cm x width 107.5 cm x thickness 5 cm

kids: How many monsters can you find pressing in on the saint?

look.text: Saint Anthony kneeling in prayer.
The seductive woman among the demons.
The burning city in the background.

timeline.text: Saint Anthony kneels in prayer while a seductive woman and a crowd of demons press in around him, a copy of the central panel of Bosch's famous Lisbon altarpiece.

title.nl: De verzoeking van de heilige Antonius de Heremiet

closer: Two doors, two different lights. Stand where you can see both at once and the room suddenly has a plan.

detail.text: De Hooch was known for the doorkijkje — the view from one room through into another — and this picture has two of them. On the left a dark opening leads down to the cellar; on the right a passage runs to the front room, where the daylight coming through the window is painted as pure white.

The child is in a dress with long bands hanging from the shoulders. Every small child wore them: they are walking reins, held by an adult behind while the child learned to stay upright. They are the sort of ordinary thing this painter noticed and almost nobody else bothered to.

displayTitle: A Maid with a Child in a Pantry
kids: The little girl has ribbons hanging off her shoulders. They are not decoration — what were they for?

look.text: The floor, laid in two colours, running the whole depth of the picture at an angle.
The far room, where the light is whitest and there is nothing at all going on.
The jug, halfway between two pairs of hands.

timeline.text: A maidservant hands a lidded jug down to a small child, on a tiled floor, between two open doorways. That is the entire event, and De Hooch has built a whole architecture around it.

title.en: A Maid with a Child in a Pantry
title.nl: Een dienstbode met een kind in een kelderkamer

closer: Look for the insects. There are more than you expect, and each one is painted at the size it really is.

detail.text: Flower painting was long established by the time Van Huysum took it up, and what he changed was the background: instead of the customary dark ground he put in a pale park — a statue of Flora at the left, some loosely brushed foliage, a pond — so the flowers seem to stand out of doors on a balustrade rather than in a closed room.

The panel is signed and dated 1723 at the lower left. Under the flowers the vase is modelled with playing putti, and at the right corner of the ledge there is a bird's nest with eggs in it, painted as carefully as anything in the bouquet.

kids: These flowers could never be in a vase together — they grow at different times of year. So how did the painter do it?

look.text: The crown imperial at the top, already going over.
The putti moulded on the side of the vase, painted as terracotta.
The butterflies and the beetle — find all of them before you move on.

timeline.text: Roses, poppies, peonies, narcissi, irises, cornflowers, fritillaries, hyacinths, a crown imperial and tulips, in one earthenware vase. None of them flower at the same time of year, so no such bouquet was ever put in a vase: it was assembled on the panel.

closer: Stand back four paces. The scrub in the foreground stops being dabs and becomes a hillside.

detail.text: What is now the main road between Nice and Monaco was a narrow mountain track when Monet walked it. The sun is high — you can tell from the walker's shadow, which is almost directly under him — and the whole picture is built out of that: red road, blue rock, green scrub, everything vibrating against everything else.

The gift came from Baroness van Lynden-van Pallandt in 1900. French Impressionism was still an oddity here; Dutch collectors of the period were buying the Hague School, which is what hangs on either side of it in this room.

name.en: The Hague School / Amsterdam impressionists / Van Gogh and contemporaries
name.nl: Haagse School / Amsterdamse impressionisten / Van Gogh en tijdgenoten

kids: What time of day is it? Look at the tiny person on the road, and at the ground next to them.

look.text: The road, which is pink, and the shadows on it, which are blue.
The headland, painted in flat slabs of violet and blue with almost no drawing.
The sea at the left, silver rather than blue, and how little of it there is.

timeline.text: A pink track climbing a Mediterranean headland at midday, painted by Monet in 1884. The museum was given it in 1900, when almost nobody in the Netherlands had heard of him, and it is the only Monet the museum currently has on view.

closer: Find the edge of the light. Rembrandt lets it fall on one small part of the picture and leaves the rest in half-tone.

detail.text: Rembrandt painted very few landscapes, and most of them are imaginary mountain country. This one is built out of thoroughly Dutch parts — a stone bridge, a hay barn, a waterway, a tower — and is very probably still invented, assembled for the light rather than observed from a spot.

It is a small panel, under thirty centimetres high, and it has been treated as a major work for two centuries: a French sale catalogue of 1817 already called its rarity and perfection remarkable despite its small size.

name.en: The young Rembrandt / The peace treaty of Münster 1648
name.nl: De jonge Rembrandt / De Vrede van Münster 1648

look.text: The lit barn and trees at the centre, and how little else is lit.
The boats on the water under the bridge.
The church tower on the horizon at the right.

timeline.text: A shaft of sunlight comes through the cloud and lands on a barn and a clump of trees, which makes the storm behind it twice as bad. Under the bridge, boats; on the road, a cart and a few people walking; in the distance to the right, a church tower.

closer: The peeled lemon in the bowl, and the whole one lying in front of it. They are the brightest things in the picture, and they are there to make the silver read as silver.

detail.text: Every object is imported or expensive: Chinese export porcelain, Amsterdam silverwork, southern fruit, a timepiece. This is a portrait of what a Dutch merchant household could afford in the 1650s, painted with the same care other painters gave to faces.

The watch is the only object that is not simply wealth. In still-life painting of the period a clock is the standard reminder that the meal, the fruit and the owner are all on a clock. The museum bought the canvas at an Amsterdam sale on 29 October 1821.

displayTitle: Still Life with a Silver Jug and a Porcelain Bowl

look.text: The curl of lemon peel in the porcelain bowl.
The figures worked into the silver of the jug, and the gilt stand under the glass.
The watch on its ribbon, half in shadow at the front edge of the ledge.

timeline.text: A few expensive things on a stone ledge, in a niche, in almost no light: an ornamented silver jug with a lid, a römer of white wine on a gilt stand, a Wan-Li porcelain bowl with lemons and oranges, and a watch. Kalf gives them the darkness a portrait painter would give a face.

title.en: Still Life with a Silver Jug and a Porcelain Bowl
title.nl: Stilleven met zilveren kan en porseleinen kom

closer: Get close. The whole picture is the difference between the white of a stalk in light and the white of the one behind it.

detail.text: Very little is known about Coorte. He is thought to have been born near Middelburg, spent about 1680 in Amsterdam as a pupil of Melchior d'Hondecoeter — whose enormous bird pieces hang two rooms away — and was back in Middelburg by 1683, signing small still lifes for the next twenty-four years. What survives is a run of them: asparagus, strawberries, gooseberries, apricots, shells, each one object on a plinth in a dark with no room in it at all. Six hang in this museum.

The fashion at the time ran the other way, towards abundance: silver, porcelain, fruit piled to the edge of the panel. These are the argument against that, and they were painted at the same moment. He signed and dated this one on the front of the plinth, in 1697.

kids: This whole painting is one bunch of vegetables. Why do you think anyone would paint that?

look.text: The string, one loop of it, holding the whole bundle and the whole composition together.
The single loose stalk lying to the right, tip broken open.
The edge of the plinth, and how little of it is lit.

timeline.text: A bundle of white asparagus tied with string, on a stone ledge, against black. Twenty-five centimetres tall and painted on paper. In a century that liked its still lifes loaded with silver and lobsters, Coorte painted one vegetable and stopped.

closer: Each king appears twice. Look above their heads, into the landscape, where all three retinues are still on the road.

detail.text: Showing the processions in miniature is the point of the picture: the kings were understood to have come from Europe, Asia and Africa, so the whole known world is arriving at one shed in the same instant.

An x-ray of the underdrawing found a change of mind. In Melchior's European train, an animal first drawn as a horse became a dromedary — surprising, because in Adoration paintings the camels usually belong to Balthasar, who was said to have come from Ethiopia. The panel's history can be traced no further back than 1904, when the museum bought it.

kids: Three kings came from three different places. Can you find all three roads?

look.text: Melchior's crown, taken off and lying on the ground.
The three retinues in the background, arriving from three directions.
The dromedary, which began as a horse.

timeline.text: The holy family shelters in a ruin at the right; the three kings arrive from the left with their gifts. Melchior kneels and offers gold, his crown on the ground at his feet. Caspar stands behind him, crown hanging at the back of his head, taking frankincense from an assistant. Balthasar, at the left, is still wearing his crown and holds an orb of myrrh.

closer: Compare the two halves. Everything Dutch is upright and lit; everything Javanese is on the ground.

detail.text: Diponegoro led the Java War of 1825 to 1830 against Dutch rule. Lieutenant General Hendrik Merkus de Kock had him seized at the peace talks and later commissioned Nicolaas Pieneman to paint the scene. What Pieneman produced shows no treachery: it shows a prince submitting. The Dutch officers stand on the veranda of the Resident's house, the tricolour is at full mast, and Diponegoro is being handed over to Major De Stuers for the carriage waiting on the left.

In the left foreground his followers sit on the ground with their weapons laid down in front of them. The museum's own note says plainly what the picture is doing and who paid for it, which is the only reason a painting like this can still be hung.

dimensions.display: height 75.8 cm x width 98.7 cm x depth 3.3 cm

kids: The man who paid for this painting is in it. Which do you think he is, and what did he want the picture to say?

look.text: Diponegoro on the steps, in a green tunic and white turban, arm raised.
The Dutch flag, and how much of the sky it is given.
The laid-down spears in the left foreground, painted as a bundle of red lines.

timeline.text: Magelang, central Java, 28 March 1830. Prince Diponegoro has come to negotiate under a promise of safe conduct and has been arrested instead. This painting was commissioned by the man who broke that promise, and it is not a record of what happened.

title.en: The Arrest of Diponegoro by Lieutenant General De Kock
title.nl: De arrestatie van Diponegoro door luitenant-generaal De Kock

attribution: Frans van der Mijn (mentioned on object)
closer: Two men, one painting, two entirely different reasons for being in it. The gesture out of the window connects them.

detail.text: Jan Pranger was director-general of the Dutch Gold Coast from 1730 to 1742. On the voyage home he travelled by way of Suriname with, in the records of the time, "170 Slaves, coming from the coast of Guinea" aboard. They were left in Paramaribo. One person was not: he came on to Amsterdam as Pranger's servant, and it was in Amsterdam that Frans van der Mijn painted the two of them together in 1742.

The picture is over two metres tall and is built entirely around Pranger: the light, the red coat, the pointing hand, the documents and inkstand on the table. The other man stands behind him in shadow, holding a parasol, and is not named anywhere.

displayTitle: Jan Pranger and an Enslaved Servant

name.en: Rococo in the Netherlands / Stadtholder Willem IV
name.nl: Rococo in Nederland / Stadhouder Willem IV

kids: There are two people here. Only one of them has a name in the title. Why do you think that is?

look.text: The hand pointing through the window at Fort Elmina.
The other man's face, the only one in the painting that is not lit.
The papers and inkstand on the table — the paperwork of the trade.

timeline.text: A man in a red coat points out of a window at a fort. The fort is Elmina, the headquarters of the Dutch slave trade in West Africa, and he ran it for twelve years. The second figure in the painting was enslaved, and the museum's title now says so.

title.en: Portrait of Jan Pranger and an Enslaved Servant
title.nl: Portret van Jan Pranger en een tot slaaf gemaakte bediende

closer: Two-thirds sky again, and this time the clouds have edges. Follow one from left to right and watch it come apart.

credit.nl: Legaat van de heer J.B.A.M. Westerwoudt, Haarlem

detail.text: The Trekvliet linked The Hague to Rijswijk and Voorburg. In the distance at the left is the tower of De Binckhorst castle; on the right is the windmill called the Laakmolen. The museum's own note makes the point that this is topography rather than invention — the Romantics before him would have moved the mill.
The painting is early Weissenbruch and still Romantic in its brightness, on a panel half a metre wide. He signed and dated it at the lower right.

name.en: The Hague School / Amsterdam impressionists / Van Gogh and contemporaries
name.nl: Haagse School / Amsterdamse impressionisten / Van Gogh en tijdgenoten

kids: Find the windmill. Then find the castle tower. They are on opposite sides.

look.text: The dark sail of the barge at the right, the one strong shape in a pale picture.
The woman with children on the farm path, painted at about a centimetre high.
The clouds, which take more than half the panel and are not repeated once.

timeline.text: The Trekvliet canal outside The Hague on a bright day in 1868, with barges under sail, a farm on the left and a woman and children on the path. Weissenbruch changed nothing: the tower on the left horizon and the mill on the right were both really there.

title.en: The Trekvliet Shipping Canal near Rijswijk, known as the ‘View near the Geest Bridge’
title.nl: De Trekvliet bij Rijswijk, bekend als ‘Gezicht bij de Geestbrug’

closer: Go looking for the insects. The museum's own description says the picture teems with them, and they are easy to walk past.

credit.nl: Aankoop met steun van de Vereniging Rembrandt

detail.text: No such bouquet ever stood on a table. There are more than ten species here and they flower at different times of the year, so the arrangement had to be assembled from study rather than observed: a year of the garden, compressed into one vase.

The insects are the second subject. Her father, Frederik Ruysch, was a professor of anatomy and botany with a vast collection of specimens, and she learned to draw on it; a fly or a beetle gets the same attention here as a petal. Her teacher, Willem van Aelst, taught her to arrange a bouquet so that it looks unarranged.

displayTitle: Still Life with Flowers on a Marble Tabletop

look.text: The blue glass of the vase, and what the marble does under it.
The insects, one by one.
How natural the arrangement looks, given that it cannot exist.

timeline.text: Roses, poppies, irises, carnations and bindweed in a blue glass vase on a marble top, signed 'Rachel Ruysch 1716'. Ruysch painted flowers professionally for more than six decades and was famous internationally in her own lifetime — the best documented woman painter of the Dutch Golden Age.

title.en: Still Life with Flowers on a Marble Tabletop
title.nl: Stilleven met bloemen op een marmeren tafelblad

closer: Everything is still except the stream. Find the moment the painting decides to hold, and you have found what Vermeer is for.

credit.en: Purchased with the support of the Vereniging Rembrandt
credit.nl: Aankoop met steun van de Vereniging Rembrandt

detail.text: She would have been called a kitchen maid rather than a milkmaid — women who milked cows were a different job — and a maid-of-all-work is not what a seventeenth-century painter gave a wall this size to. The canvas is 45.5 by 41 centimetres, which is small; the figure inside it is not.

The museum's own note points at the light: hundreds of coloured dots laid over the surface of things, so that the bread crusts stay rough and the maid's forearms stay heavy. Half her face is in shadow, and neither her eyes nor her mouth will say whether she is concentrating or thinking about something else entirely.

Behind her, low on the wall, runs a row of Delft tiles — Cupid on the left of them, a figure with a pole on the right — and a wooden foot warmer sits on the floor. Kitchen maids carried a reputation in Dutch painting for being inclined to love, and those two objects are how the picture mentions it without saying it.

kids: Everything in this room is standing still except one thing. What is it?

look.text: The stream of milk, the one thing in the picture that is moving.
The crust of the bread, built up in dabs of paint thick enough to throw their own shadows.
The bare wall: most of the right-hand half of the picture is plaster, light and nothing else.

timeline.text: A kitchen maid pours milk into an earthenware bowl and nothing else in the room moves. Vermeer took the plainest job in the house and painted it at the scale and seriousness of an altarpiece: she stands like a statue, and the only thing falling is the milk.

closer: The archaeology is the point and also the alibi. Underneath it, one person is doubled over on a stone floor.

credit.en: Gift of Mr and Mrs Drucker-Fraser, Montreux
credit.nl: Schenking van de heer en mevrouw Drucker-Fraser, Montreux

detail.text: Alma-Tadema was Frisian, moved to England, was knighted there, and became one of the most popular painters of the nineteenth century on the strength of pictures like this: the ancient world reconstructed detail by detail, and then a single ordinary emotion put in the middle of it.

He painted this in 1872, on panel, and signed it on the sarcophagus. The Egyptian architecture, the painted columns, the inlaid floor and the instruments are all worked up from what was known at the time — which is why the picture is also a document of what 1872 believed Egypt had looked like.

kids: Everyone here is sad about the same thing. Which person looks the saddest, and why?

look.text: The mourner, the only figure whose face you cannot see.
The painted mummy case, with a face on the lid.
The harp at the right, and the row of musicians beside it.

timeline.text: A woman crouches in a temple beside the inner case holding her husband's body, her face in her hands. Priests and singers perform the lament at the right; the empty sarcophagus stands at the left. Everything in the room has been researched.

closer: Walk towards it until the dots become a field, then take one step back. That distance is what the painting is about.

credit.en: Gift of B. Hart Nibbrig, Hilversum
credit.nl: Schenking van B. Hart Nibbrig, Hilversum

detail.text: This is pointillism, arrived in the Netherlands about twenty-five years after Paris invented it. The method is to put unmixed colours side by side and let the eye do the mixing, and it works best on exactly this sort of subject: strong light, flat land and a great deal of green needing to stay alive across a metre and a half.

Hart Nibbrig signed it at the lower right. The dune the view is taken from is doing the same work as the sky in a seventeenth-century Dutch landscape — it puts the horizon low and lets the village sit in the middle distance, small.

kids: Get close to the painting and then walk backwards. What happens to the little dots?

look.text: The dune grass in the foreground, where the touches are largest and the colours least mixed.
The sea at the left, made of green, blue and white dots and no line at all.
The red roofs of the village, the only warm colour in the picture.

timeline.text: The village of Zoutelande on Walcheren, seen from the top of a dune: sea on the left, roofs and a mill on the right, and the whole thing built out of separate dabs of colour that never touch. Painted between 1910 and 1912, a metre and a half wide.

title.nl: Gezicht op het dorp Zoutelande op Walcheren

closer: Christ is standing among the onlookers in every panel. Once you have found him in one, you will find him in the rest.

credit.en: Purchased with the support of the Vereniging Rembrandt and the Commissie voor Fotoverkoop
credit.nl: Aankoop met steun van de Vereniging Rembrandt en de Commissie voor Fotoverkoop

detail.text: The acts come from Matthew 25, where they decide the Last Judgement — which is why the Judgement is painted in the upper centre of the middle panel. The series was probably commissioned by the Holy Ghost confraternity of Alkmaar, whose members ran a house where the sick were cared for and travellers put up: the seven scenes are the work they actually did.

The panels have been attacked. Faces were cut away with a sharp tool, before 1582 and probably during the iconoclasm of 1566; in 1582 two men painted the whole thing over in black. When the museum, which bought the work in 1918, had it restored between 1971 and 1975, it decided not to fill the losses in. What you are looking at is the damage as well as the painting.

Aertsen paints the game being attempted and everyone else occupied with something less innocent — the man at the left raising a jug over his head, the couple sprawled across the bench beside him, the bagpiper at the fire.

Pictures like this were sold as entertainment and defended as morality. The date 1552 is painted on the chimney breast above the fire. The panel is nearly a metre and three quarters wide: a tavern interior given the scale of a history painting.

detail.text: The format — curtain, parapet, distant view — is what Titian and Rembrandt had used, and Steen is claiming it. He changed his mind repeatedly while doing so. Infrared shows three versions of the collar: a very broad one, then a knotted cravat in the fashion of about 1668, then the plain white bef he settled on. The left eye was once larger and set higher, and the mouth was once a wider grin, painted out in favour of the drier smile that is there now.

The 1995 restoration is what made all this legible. Before it, an overpainted brown background sat round his head like a cloud; underneath were the red curtain with its tasselled cord and a landscape painted wet into wet that looks oddly like the work of his father-in-law Jan van Goyen. The one loose end is the balustrade, which does not continue on the left.

detail.text: Sinterklaas has been kept in more or less this form for centuries: good children get presents from the saint, bad ones get a birch rod in their shoe. The boy on the left got the rod. His grandmother is beckoning him from behind the bed curtain — there is something for him after all, hidden there — and the laughing boy beside their mother, with a kolf stick in his hand, is enjoying the situation far too much.

Steen was a storyteller before he was anything else, and he has got every part of the festival into one room: the bucket of treats, the doll of John the Baptist in the girl's arms, the basket of bread and spiced biscuit on the floor, the children singing by the chimney where the saint is supposed to come down.

kids: One child in this picture is crying. Can you find out why — and who is trying to cheer him up?

look.text: The crying boy, and the shoe he found the rod in.
The basket on the floor: bread, apples, and a long moulded speculaas figure.
The girl's face, which knows exactly how well she has done.

timeline.text: The morning of the sixth of December, and the presents have been handed out unevenly. The small girl in the middle has a bucket of sweets and a doll and will not let either go. Her brother, on the left, has been crying since he looked in his shoe.

closer: The background is one colour, laid on flat. Everything the picture does, it does with the head.

detail.text: Van Scorel spent 1518 to 1524 in Italy, and his stay happened to coincide with the reign of the only Dutch pope, Adrian VI, who made him court painter and put him in charge of the papal antiquities. He came back one of the first northern painters to have absorbed the Italian manner at first hand, and the solidity of this head is what he brought home.

The arched top is not a frame: it is the shape of the panel, cut that way. Against it the red ground pushes the head forward, which is the whole device — no interior, no landscape, nothing behind him at all.

kids: We do not know this man's name. What can you work out about him just from looking?

look.text: The hands, held together at the bottom edge, doing nothing in particular.
The fur lining of the coat, painted stroke by stroke.
The eyes, which are looking somewhere past your shoulder.

timeline.text: An unnamed man from Haarlem, painted by Jan van Scorel in 1529 on an arched panel against flat orange-red. No coat of arms, no motto, no attributes. Just a face, and a fur-lined coat he is holding shut.

closer: Find the eagle. Everything about the picture changes once you have.

detail.text: This is a wall, not a picture. It is a fragment of a painted room decoration, made in 1727 for Jan Baptist de Surmont, lord of Vlooswijk, for his house at Loenen aan de Vecht, and it is two and a half metres tall. Its companion piece hangs beside it.

De Wit spent his career painting rooms — ceilings, overdoors, wall pieces, several more of them elsewhere on this floor — in a light, high-keyed manner made for living in rather than for looking at across a gallery. He signed and dated this on the rock in the middle, below the eagle. Around the edges of the scene the props of the disguise are laid out: Diana's hunting gear at the lower right, her dogs beside it, a quiver hanging in the tree, and putti at the left with more of the same.

The quiver of arrows hanging from the tree, with a putto climbing to it.
The red drape, which is doing the job a curtain does on a stage.

timeline.text: Jupiter has disguised himself as the goddess Diana in order to get close to the nymph Callisto, and the two women on the ground are one god and one victim. The eagle behind the rock, holding thunderbolts, is the giveaway.

title.en: Jupiter, Disguised as Diana, Seducing the Nymph Callisto

closer: The feathers nearest you are laid on thickly enough to cast their own shadow. The dog, by contrast, is barely there.

detail.text: Someone later decided the swan was Johan de Witt, the Grand Pensionary, defending Holland against its enemies, and wrote the reading onto the painting: ‘de Raad-Pensionaris’ under the swan, ‘Holland’ on the egg, ‘de viand van de staat’ above the dog. Asselijn did not put them there — he died in 1652, and the inscriptions are now thought to date from the 1750s, from a pamphlet war. His own mark is the monogram ‘JA’ at the lower right.

It was under that political meaning that the picture became the first purchase of the Nationale Konst-Gallery, the forerunner of this museum, in 1800, for a hundred guilders. The collection you are standing in began with a hissing bird.

kids: The swan is much bigger than the dog. Who do you think wins?

look.text: The three inscriptions, which turn a swan into a statesman.
The near feathers, thick enough to throw shadows onto the ones behind.
The dog, deliberately vague — he is a threat, not a subject.

timeline.text: A swan defends her nest against a dog, wings out, hissing, at close to life size — the canvas is 144 by 171 centimetres. Asselijn gave an animal picture the scale and front-on force of a history painting, and it works on anyone who walks past it without reading a word.

closer: Her face is turned away and the picture is built so that it stays that way. Everything you want to know is behind that head.

detail.text: The old title calls it a father admonishing his daughter, which the picture does not support: the man is an officer, still holding his hat as though he has just come in, and the woman with the glass is nobody's chaperone. The museum's own note goes no further than saying the reason for the gathering remains obscure. Ter Borch liked scenes whose point cannot be pinned down, and this is the most unpinnable of them.

What he could do without ambiguity is cloth. The satin dress is the reason people stop here — the folds are painted in long dragged strokes of grey, white and pale gold that change direction with the fall of the skirt, and nothing else in the room is given anything like the same attention.

The officer's raised hand — the gesture the old title depends on.
The dog at the right, sitting out the conversation.

timeline.text: A woman in white satin stands with her back to us. A seated officer is saying something to her, one hand raised; a second woman drinks from a glass and does not look up. What is going on here has never been settled.

detail.text: Paul is identified in art by a sword and by the epistles he wrote, and both are here: the blade shows where the cloak falls open, the pages are in his hands. Putting his own head on the apostle was a way of pulling the viewer up close to a figure who would otherwise stay at scripture's distance.

It is one of more than forty painted self-portraits, and among the last. Ernst van de Wetering read the surface as wet-on-wet work: the turban gone at speed, the lit forehead built up thick enough for the paint itself to make the wrinkles. The signature and the date 1661 are written across the shadowed wall on the left.

kids: He has dressed up as someone from the Bible. What has he put on his head?

look.text: The forehead, where the paint is heaped up and doing the work of skin.
The pages, curling at the top edge and catching the only other light in the picture.
The eyes, which are looking at a mirror and therefore straight at you.

timeline.text: Rembrandt at fifty-five, in a white turban, holding a bundle of letters and wearing a sword under his cloak. The turban and the sword and the manuscript belong to the Apostle Paul. The face is entirely his own, and he has not flattered it.

closer: The clothes give it away. Nobody in Amsterdam dressed like this in the 1630s — the costume is borrowed from earlier centuries.

detail.text: The face has the domed forehead, slightly protruding eyes and pronounced chin that recur in Rembrandt's goddesses and heroines of the same years. That is an argument for a type rather than a likeness, and it is why the picture was renamed.
What is not in doubt is the jewellery. A thin veil over the hair, pearl earrings, a rope of pearls at the throat, all painted at a size where you can see how each one is made of two or three strokes.

look.text: The veil, and how little paint it takes.
The pearls at the ear and the throat.
The costume, which belongs to no decade she lived in.

timeline.text: She was long called Saskia van Uylenburgh, Rembrandt's wife, and the museum's own record still says the sitter may be her. The title has changed because this is not strictly a portrait: it is a tronie, a fantasy head, painted in 1633.

detail.text: Cuyp was born and died in Dordrecht, was taught by his father and is known above all for large river views in a golden early-morning or late-afternoon light. That light is what he is doing here: coming in low from one side, it turns every upright thing into a silhouette with a gilded edge. The hill it falls on is not a Dutch hill.

He signed it at the bottom centre. It was bought for the nation with support from the Vereniging Rembrandt, and hangs in the Gallery of Honour among the pictures the museum puts at the front of the queue.

timeline.text: Two riders have stopped at the edge of a river and one horse is drinking. Behind them a hillside goes gold in low sun, cattle stand about, and a town shows its towers in the far distance. The canvas is over two metres wide and almost all of it is light.

detail.text: The museum's note says the picture is based on a Nativity with half-length figures known in versions in Brussels and Cologne. The Amsterdam panel gained a group of music-making angels above the crib, which gives it its horizontal shape. Those angels also appear in fifteenth-century Nativities by Hugo van der Goes.

The ox and the donkey stand by the trough. A shepherd peeps from behind a curtain. Two men warm themselves at a fire on the left, and in the distance on the right is the annunciation to the shepherds.

detail.text: Troost worked as an actor and a scene painter before making his living with a brush, and what he understood from that trade was illusion. The oval, the drape, the pedestal and the objects laid on it are there to build depth in front of a head that is otherwise simply a head, seen — as he tells you — in a mirror.

He signed and dated it 1739: C. Troost ipse fecit, made by himself. The showpiece is the jabot at his throat, the frill of fine batiste on his shirt, which the museum's own note points out is a single stroke of white paint.

kids: Is that gold frame a real frame, or did he paint it? How can you tell?

look.text: The palette on the ledge, with the colours set out along its edge.
The drawing on blue paper, hanging over the front edge into your space.
The brown curtain, drawn back at the left and doing all the work of depth.

timeline.text: A painter looks out of an oval gold frame that is itself painted, past a curtain that is also painted, over a ledge where his palette and brushes are lying. Troost had been an actor before he was a painter, and this is a piece of stagecraft.

closer: The two oak planks have cracked at top and bottom, and the varnish has discoloured. The scene reads dimmer now than it was painted.

detail.text: The moment is John 19: Pilate shows Christ, crowned with thorns, to the people, saying "Behold the man". The painting is a fairly faithful copy of the Ecce Homo in Frankfurt, painted around 1480-1490 and commonly accepted as an early work by Bosch.
The original carried the words in gold lettering: "Ecce Homo", "Crucifige eum" (Crucify him), and an appeal to the Redeemer on the corner of the rostrum. This copy leaves those inscriptions out.

timeline.text: Pilate presents the thorn-crowned Christ to a jeering crowd, a scene Bosch painted early in his career and his followers copied for decades.

detail.text: Claesz signed and dated it 1627, monogram and year cut into the blade of the knife at the front of the table. It is among the largest and most ambitious things he painted, and it belongs to the moment when Dutch still life turned from modest breakfast pieces to displays of imported luxury.

Much of what is on the table came a long way. The fruit bowl is Chinese Wan-li porcelain; the cup beside it is a tropical shell set in a gilt mount; the flagons are pewter and silver. The white damask, the oriental carpet under it and the low viewpoint are all doing the same work as the imports.

look.text: The turkey's head, still attached, propped up over the pie like a hat ornament.
The oysters, each one a different shade of grey and each one lit separately.
The knife at the front edge, carrying the date and the painter's initials.

timeline.text: A pie with a whole turkey reassembled on top of it — skin, wings and head — set among oysters, lemons, olives, nuts, a nautilus cup and a Chinese porcelain bowl of grapes. Nobody ate like this. The table is an argument about what its owner could afford.

detail.text: Rembrandt fills the room with the evidence of their poverty: a string of onions and a birdcage by the window, shelves of household things along the back wall, a basket in a niche, a spool of yarn left on a chair, a stick on the floor beside him, a small dog at the fire. Anna stands holding the goat and says nothing.

He was barely twenty when he painted it, and the picture is already about the wrong conclusion drawn in a moment. In the Book of Tobit the couple's fortunes are restored, but that is not the part he chose.

She has come home with a goat she was paid with, he hears it bleating and accuses her of stealing it, and he is praying to be allowed to die.

detail.text: That is the trick of the picture, and probably of the sitter. Everything reads as restraint — black cloth, white linen, no jewellery worth mentioning — and everything is expensive. Sober dress was how a certain kind of Dutch money preferred to be seen.

The two portraits were painted as a pair and hung as a pair, and they have been apart for long enough that the museum's record has to explain the absence. Buying this one back took a consortium: the state, the Vereniging Rembrandt, four foundations, a lottery, businesses and private donors.

detail.text: It was not the church that ordered this. Abraham Anthonisz Recht, an Amsterdam merchant and an admirer, commissioned the portrait and hung it in his own house — a private statement of loyalty to a man on the wrong side of an argument the state had settled.

The open book leaning against the wall marks him as a man of the Word. Nobody has identified the text. The museum bought the painting in December 1992 for £4,180,000, with the Vereniging Rembrandt, three funds, the Dutch state and private collectors.

Johannes Wtenbogaert led the Remonstrants, the losing side of the religious conflict that split the young Dutch Republic. Rembrandt painted him in 1633 and wrote his age on the canvas: 'Aet:.76'.

detail.text: Maes began as a Rembrandt pupil painting dark interiors and old women — the praying old woman a few rooms from here is his — went home to Dordrecht for twenty years, and came back to Amsterdam to become the leading portrait painter of the city's last decades of the century. This is that late manner: a knee-length pose against a park, blue dress, orange wrap, painted between 1677 and 1685.
It is one of a pair. Petronella Dunois married Pieter Groenendijk in 1677, and Maes painted him too; the two portraits belong together.

kids: She had a dolls' house, and it is in this room. Which do you think cost more — the house or the painting?

The shawl, one long slab of orange with the folds cut into it.
The pearls, three or four strokes each.

timeline.text: A woman leaning on a low wall in an orange shawl, holding a sprig of apple blossom. Her dolls' house — the museum still files it under her name — stands in this same room, a few paces from her face.

closer: The two ribbons on his chest. The blue one is the Aceh Medal; the green and orange is the Cross for Important Military Service.

detail.text: He served twelve years and fought in the Aceh War in Sumatra, one of the longest and bloodiest campaigns of the Dutch colonial era. Isaac Israels painted him in 1882, in the Netherlands, while he was on sick leave and shortly before he went back to Africa.

Almost everything about him reaches us through Dutch paperwork: a European name given at a recruiting post, medals awarded by the army he was recruited into, a rank and a campaign. The portrait is here because the museum now shows that history rather than storing it.

detail.text: Jan Steen dated it 1655 and set it precisely: the tower of the Oude Kerk stands behind, and the bridge over the Oude Delft carries the arms of the town. For most of its life the sitters were unknown and the picture went under the name 'The Burgomaster of Delft and his Daughter' — a title it has kept in speech although the man was never the burgomaster. Research on the cityscape and the sitters in 2006 identified them as Adolf Croeser and his daughter Catharina.

It hung at Penrhyn Castle in Wales for over a century. The Rijksmuseum bought it in July 2004 for 11.9 million euros, the most it has ever paid for a painting, after the British government held back the export licence to give British institutions a chance to match the offer.

detail.text: The museum calls it the first painting to show Spanish soldiers subduing the people who lived there. Mostaert worked in Haarlem all his life and knew the subject only from report, so the setting is an ordinary European landscape with exotica added to it: a monkey, a porcupine, parrots.
It is his most famous painting and it took a coalition to buy it: the lottery, the Vereniging Rembrandt, three national funds, and the family of the dealer Jacques Goudstikker, in his memory.

timeline.text: A wide hilly landscape under a great rock, and a battle running through it. Indigenous people with bows, sticks and flails are defending themselves against Spanish troops with lances, halberds, firearms and cannon. Mostaert painted it around 1535, in Haarlem, without ever having crossed the Atlantic.

detail.text: An ensign carried the colours of a civic guard company and was expected to die rather than lose them. Rembrandt gives him a column at his back — a standard emblem of steadfastness — a gorget at his throat, a sword, and sixteenth-century dress with slashed sleeves that was already costume by 1636. The light comes hard from the upper left and lands on the banner and on his right cuff.

The Dutch State bought the painting in 2021, with the Vereniging Rembrandt and its members contributing, after it had spent generations in the Rothschild collection in Paris. It had been described as a self-portrait as early as 1836; the face under the moustache is the one from all the other self-portraits.

detail.text: Dou trained with Rembrandt in Leiden from the age of fourteen and then went the other way entirely, into the small, polished manner of the Leiden fijnschilders. He is said to have spent five days painting a hand, and to have made his own brushes because none he could buy were fine enough. The stone niche with a sill is the device he is known for, and the whole point of it is to let things lean out at the viewer.

The book on the ledge overhangs the stone and reaches into the room; the curtain hangs from rings on a rod, so that at first glance it is the curtain over the picture rather than a part of it. The signature is on the sheet of paper below the book.

detail.text: The town hall went up in the middle of the seventeenth century, when Amsterdam had more money than any city in Europe, and it was designed to say so: classical, symmetrical, enormous, with a cupola over the middle. Berckheyde painted it repeatedly, and here he takes it head on and gives it two-thirds of the canvas.

Everything else is compressed around it. The Nieuwe Kerk crowds in at the right, the gabled houses of the Damrak at the left, and across the paving are pedlars, a dog, a wheelbarrow, riders and a knot of people bargaining. The signature and the date are at the lower left.

detail.text: The cupboard is the point. In a household of this class the linen press was the store of the family's most valuable movable goods, and the mistress of the house carried its key and handed out the sheets. Painting a woman at an open linen cupboard is painting a woman in charge of something.

Everything else is arranged around that transaction: the child at her game, the light from the street, the small sculpture on the doorframe. Nothing dramatic happens, and the whole composition is engineered so that you notice.

detail.text: Maritge Vooght came from Haarlem brewers and married Pieter Olycan at eighteen. The marriage let him take high office in the town and made him co-heir to her family's brewery; the couple then founded a second brewery of their own, registered — as the period required — in his name alone. Their daughter Geertruyt ran the business on.

The portrait is a knee-length seated one, and probably the companion to a portrait of her husband now in Sarasota. The wealth is stated by the clothing and by the book, which has silver corner mounts and a silver clasp and is the most expensive object in the picture.

detail.text: De Hooch made a speciality of the doorkijkje, the through-view: a second room, seen past a door frame, lit from a source the near room cannot reach. Here it does more than show off. The far room is bright, empty and quiet; the near one is shadowed and busy with an unglamorous chore, and the two rooms are held together by a line of sunlight lying across both floors.

The furnishings are ordinary and exactly observed: Delft blue tiles along the wall, a box bed with its pillows stacked, a wicker basket, and in the right foreground a kakstoel — a child's potty chair. A dog sits watching the open door.

Ter Borch painted the ratification itself: the delegates of both sides around one table, named one by one in the museum's record, with the treaty documents lying in their boxes on the green cloth in front of them.

He signed it on the painted wall at the upper left, "made at Münster, 1648". He also put himself in: the figure at the extreme left edge, looking out of the picture, is the painter. The support is copper, which is why the detail holds at this scale.

detail.text: Avercamp's earlier ice scenes are bird's-eye views crowded with tiny figures — his Winter Landscape with Ice Skaters, elsewhere in this museum, is one. By 1620 that had opened out into broad frozen channels and flooded fields, with the trees and buildings pushed to the margins and the figures given the picture.

The people in the immediate foreground are the largest and the most sharply drawn, and they are a cross-section: different classes on the same ice, each doing what its class did there. Further back the drawing softens deliberately, and the groups are strung out along diagonals that pull the eye into the distance.

The white is confined to the collar and the cuffs, and the gold chain running out of her hand is close to the only warm colour in the canvas.

detail.text: He was about thirty-five when he moved south, and the stay was prolific: in under 444 days at Arles he made about a hundred drawings, more than two hundred paintings, and wrote more than two hundred letters. The wheat harvest of June 1888 gave him a run of canvases, and on 21 June he described them to his brother Theo as landscapes "yellow — old gold — done quickly, quickly, quickly, and in a hurry just like the harvester who is silent under the blazing sun, intent only on the reaping".

The sky is laid in long horizontal strokes and the field in short upright ones, so the two halves of the picture are different weather to the hand as well as to the eye. What stands between them is a thin strip of the world: a white farmhouse with an orange roof, a haystack, sheds, a row of dark trees at the right-hand edge, and the blue line of the hills behind all of it.

detail.text: Almost everyone here has a name — the museum lists two dozen of them, from the ensign Jacob Banningh sitting beside the big drum down to Willem the drummer — and most of the objects on the table have survived as well. That is unusual even among civic-guard portraits, and it is why this canvas is used as evidence about how such dinners actually looked.

Paper hangs on the drum with a poem by Jan Vos on it, spelling out the occasion for anyone who needed telling. Through the open windows you can see the front of the brewery 'het Lam' on the Singel. The painting is dated 1648, but historians think it was finished a year or more later; van der Helst seems to have dated his group portraits from the commission, not the completion.

detail.text: Seymour Slive, who catalogued Ruisdael's paintings, noted that the detail holds up to specialist reading: the set of the sails and the movement of the water are both correct. The canvas is signed 'Ruisdael' at the lower right but carries no date — Ruisdael dated almost nothing after 1653 — so the museum gives it as about 1668 to 1670.

The mill is gone; its foundations can still be seen. Another mill a few hundred metres away is regularly mistaken for it, a confusion that goes back to a description published in 1911. The painting itself belongs to the City of Amsterdam, from the Van der Hoop bequest, and has been on loan to the Rijksmuseum since 1885.

displayTitle: The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede

look.text: The signature at the lower right, on the bank.
The women walking along the bank, who set the scale for the mill.
The bank of cloud, and where it lets the sun through.

timeline.text: The mill takes the whole picture. The Lek comes in from the left with a boat on it, the towers of Kasteel Duurstede and the Sint-Janskerk stand in the distance, and a working mill is painted taller than either of them.

title.en: The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede
title.nl: De molen bij Wijk bij Duurstede

closer: Stand close enough to see the gold sleeve as paint. It is trowelled on, then scratched into with the wrong end of the brush.

credit.en: On loan from the City of Amsterdam (A. van der Hoop Bequest)
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de gemeente Amsterdam (legaat A. van der Hoop)

detail.text: The title is a nineteenth-century mistake that stuck. An Amsterdam collector decided the scene showed a Jewish father fastening a necklace on his daughter's wedding day; nobody accepts that now, and no replacement has won. The museum reads the pair as Isaac and Rebecca, who told King Abimelech they were brother and sister so that Isaac would not be killed for her, and were given away by exactly this kind of unguarded moment. Rembrandt had drawn that subject some years earlier. Others have proposed his son Titus, or the poet Miguel de Barrios, or Abraham and Sarah, or Boaz and Ruth.

What is not in doubt is the handling. The gold of the man's sleeve is laid on in ridges thick enough to catch the gallery light and then cut into while still wet, and her red skirt is worked the same way. Rembrandt's biographer Christopher White called the result one of the greatest expressions in painting of spiritual and physical love fused together, which is a large claim that the picture does not obviously fail.

kids: The two people are touching in three places. Can you find all three?

look.text: His hand on her chest, and her hand laid over it — neither gripping, both deciding.
The sleeve: gold paint standing off the canvas in ridges, scored with a blunt point.
Her face, which is doing something quieter and harder to name than his.

timeline.text: A man lays his hand on a woman's breast and she lays hers on top of it, and that is the whole event. Nobody knows for certain who they are. The picture survives the not knowing, because what it is actually about is two hands agreeing.

title.en: Isaac and Rebecca, Known as ‘The Jewish Bride’
title.nl: Isaak en Rebekka, bekend als ‘Het Joodse bruidje’

closer: It looks like an argument for a good evening. Read the note on the mantelpiece and it turns into a warning.

credit.en: On loan from the City of Amsterdam (A. van der Hoop Bequest)
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de gemeente Amsterdam (legaat A. van der Hoop)

detail.text: Steen painted this in 1668, and the proverb it illustrates was old already. Everything in the room is an example being set: the man playing bagpipes, the old man's raised roemer of wine, the boy leaning out of the window on the left, the two smallest children at the front being handed a pipe to try.

The trouble with the argument is that the evening looks like a good one. Steen has made the wrong example far more attractive than the lesson, which is why the picture has outlasted the proverb it was painted to carry.

kids: Count how many people in this room are making a noise. Is anyone being quiet?

look.text: The note above the fireplace, which is the sentence the painting is illustrating.
The boy in the window on the far left, blowing a pipe out into the street.
The dog under the table, the only member of the household not joining in.

timeline.text: Father is singing with a full glass in his hand, mother and grandmother are singing with him, and the children are learning the tune. A sheet of paper pinned above the fireplace gives the moral: as the old sing, so the young pipe.

closer: There is no wind in this picture. Find every place Van de Velde tells you so.

credit.en: On loan from the City of Amsterdam (A. van der Hoop Bequest)
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de gemeente Amsterdam (legaat A. van der Hoop)

detail.text: Van de Velde the Younger grew up in the trade. His father was a marine draughtsman who made studies of naval actions, and the son worked from them; he was also taught by Simon de Vlieger and looked hard at Jan van de Cappelle, who painted clouds and their reflections in still water. All of that is in this picture, spent on stillness: the sails loosed and empty, the sea a sheet, the hull sitting in its own reflection.

Two sloops lie to either side of the man-of-war, and a second Dutch ship rides in the distance with its sails down. The picture is the companion to another Van de Velde in this museum, a ship caught in a squall — the same painter's answer to the opposite weather.

dimensions.display: height 78.5 cm x width 67 cm x height 90.8 cm x width 80.5 cm x depth 7.5 cm

kids: The ship is firing a gun, but nobody is fighting. Why do you think it is doing that?

look.text: The smoke, the only fast-moving thing in the painting.
The carved and gilded stern, painted at a size where every figure on it still reads.
The reflection under the hull, which is how you know how still the water is.

timeline.text: A Dutch warship lying in a flat calm, sails hanging slack, firing a single gun. Nothing is being attacked and nothing is moving. The whole painting is arranged around the cloud of smoke that one shot makes.

closer: The blue is the whole picture. Once you notice how far it reaches — jacket, chair, tablecloth, the shadows on the wall — the room stops being a room and becomes a colour.

credit.en: On loan from the City of Amsterdam (A. van der Hoop Bequest)
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de gemeente Amsterdam (legaat A. van der Hoop)

detail.text: This was the first Vermeer the Rijksmuseum had. It came with the Van der Hoop bequest to the City of Amsterdam in 1854 and hung here from the museum's opening in 1885; it is still the City's, on loan. The painted canvas is 46.5 by 39 centimetres — the sizes the museum lists for it are the framed ones.

The map behind her is a real one — Holland and West Friesland, drawn by Balthasar Florisz. van Berckenrode and published in 1620 — and Vermeer used it in other pictures too. Because it hangs where the far corner of the room would be, the painting is the only interior of his in which no corner, no floor and no ceiling can be seen at all: the woman stands against a flat wall of paper and plaster.

Whether she is pregnant has been argued over for a century. The loose jacket was the fashion, and Dutch painting of the period almost never showed pregnancy, so the roundness may be the cut of the cloth. The picture declines to settle it, which is consistent with everything else it declines to settle.

kids: She is reading a letter. Who do you think sent it, and what does it say?

look.text: The letter, held in both hands, and her lips just parted around a word.
The blue jacket, the largest single thing in the painting.
The brass nail heads on the chair back, picked out one at a time in the near dark.

timeline.text: A young woman stands in morning light, still in her blue night jacket, reading a letter that arrived before she was dressed. Vermeer gives away nothing of what it says and everything about how it is being read.

closer: Look along the row and find the seam. The left-hand men are alive in a way the right-hand men are not.

credit.en: On loan from the City of Amsterdam
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de gemeente Amsterdam

detail.text: Hals was commissioned in 1633 on the strength of his Haarlem militia pieces, and the picture is dated 1637 — four years for a job he had done in months before. Every sitter paid for his own place on the canvas, which is one reason a group portrait of this kind could stall: it was a dozen separate transactions pretending to be a painting.

The composition and roughly the seven figures on the left are held to be largely Hals's. Codde matched the style closely enough that the join is a matter of argument rather than of sight, but the brushwork on the left is looser and the faces there do more.

dimensions.display: support: height 209 cm x width 429 cm

kids: This painting has a nickname: the Meagre Company. Look at the men. Do you think it is fair?

look.text: The flag bearer at the far left, in a slashed sleeve, with the orange banner behind him.
The blue-and-white sashes, which run the whole width of the picture at the same height.
The forest of pikes and halberds above the heads, holding the top of the canvas together.

timeline.text: The only militia piece Frans Hals ever painted outside Haarlem, and it nearly did not get painted at all. He travelled to Amsterdam repeatedly; sitters failed to turn up; he demanded they come to him instead; they refused and hired Pieter Codde to finish it.

title.en: Militia Company of District XI under the Command of Captain Reynier Reael
title.nl: Schutters van wijk XI onder leiding van kapitein Reynier Reael

closer: Follow the captain's outstretched hand. Its shadow falls across the lieutenant's gold coat, and that single detail fixes the two men in real space.

credit.en: On loan from the City of Amsterdam
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de gemeente Amsterdam

detail.text: The company belongs to District II of Amsterdam's civic guard, and the painting hung in their hall on the Kloveniersburgwal before moving to the town hall in 1715. It was cut down to fit that wall, losing figures from the left side and part of the arch behind. Rembrandt signed and dated it 1642.

What the militiamen bought was novelty, and it is still the reason the picture works. Group portraits of the period line their sitters up so each paid face is equally legible. Rembrandt subordinated all eighteen to a single moment of movement — a drum starting up, a musket going off, a dog barking — and let some of them fall into shadow to do it.

dimensions.display: height 379.5 cm x width 453.5 cm x weight 337 kg x weight 170 kg

kids: Find the dog, the drum, and the girl with a chicken hanging from her belt.

look.text: The captain's hand and the shadow it throws onto the lieutenant's coat.
The girl in gold behind the captain, with a chicken hanging from her belt — its claws are the militia's emblem.
The light: count the sources. There is no single sun in this picture.

timeline.text: Eighteen militiamen paid to appear in a group portrait and Rembrandt gave them a scene instead. Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, in black, is telling his lieutenant to march the company out; everyone else is still catching up with the order. It is not a night scene — the dark came from centuries of varnish, since removed.

title.en: The Night Watch Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq

closer: The joke and the reverence are in the same picture and neither cancels the other. That is harder to do than it looks.

credit.en: On loan from the City of Amsterdam
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de gemeente Amsterdam

detail.text: The Dutch title — het gebed zonder end, the prayer without end — is the name of the joke: she prays, the meal goes. Maes painted it around 1656, a few years after leaving Rembrandt's studio, and the debt shows in the light, which comes from one side and leaves most of the room in brown darkness.

In the niche behind her is a small still life doing quiet work: a bunch of keys, a funnel and an hourglass. The hourglass is time running out, and it is hanging directly above an old woman at her last meal of the day.

kids: She has her eyes shut. Something in the room is taking advantage of that. What is it?

look.text: Her hands, the lightest thing in the painting after the tablecloth.
The cat, with a claw already in the linen.
The niche: keys, funnel, hourglass, all painted as carefully as she is.

timeline.text: An old woman says grace over bread, fish, cheese and a jug, eyes closed, hands folded. At the right-hand edge of the table, out of her sight, a cat has got hold of the cloth and is pulling.

title.en: Old Woman Saying Grace, Known as ‘The Prayer without End’
title.nl: Oude vrouw in gebed, bekend als ‘Het gebed zonder end’

closer: The fan in her left hand is Chinese and folds. In 1639 that was a rare and expensive thing to be holding.

credit.en: On loan from the Familie Van Weede Stichting
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de Familie Van Weede Stichting

detail.text: Rembrandt gives the jewellery everything he has: each pearl is a stroke of grey and a stroke of white, and from two metres away they hang and swing. The lace is done the same way, as pattern implied rather than drawn.

The identification is likely rather than proven, which is why the museum's title says 'probably'. What is certain is the money, and that a painter who could handle it this well was the one an Amsterdam family of that class would go to.

displayTitle: Portrait of a Woman, Probably Maria Trip

name.en: The young Rembrandt / The peace treaty of Münster 1648
name.nl: De jonge Rembrandt / De Vrede van Münster 1648

look.text: The pearls, first from across the room and then from close up.
The folding fan, held out at her hip.
The lace collar, and how few actual lines it is made of.

timeline.text: She was about twenty, and her family sold arms. Maria Trip stands with one arm on a balustrade, wearing a collar of the finest lace, a brooch with earrings to match, and a fortune in pearls — at the ear, at the throat, on the wrists.

title.en: Portrait of a Woman, Probably Maria Trip (1619-1683)
title.nl: Portret van een vrouw, waarschijnlijk Maria Trip

closer: They are all looking at you and none of them is posing. Work out how he managed both at once and you have the picture.

credit.en: On loan from the City of Amsterdam
credit.nl: Bruikleen van de gemeente Amsterdam

detail.text: The sitters were the wardens of the Amsterdam drapers' guild, whose job was to test cloth against sample pieces — staal in Dutch, which is where their name comes from. Quality ran to four grades, marked by pressing one to four seals into small lead slugs attached to the bolt. The post was unpaid and honorary, the term ran a year from Good Friday, and this board met three times a week. They were, between them, two Catholics, a Mennonite, a Remonstrant and a Reformed Protestant. From the left: Jacob van Loon, Volckert Jansz, Willem van Doeyenburg, the servant Frans Hendricksz Bel standing behind, Aernout van der Mye and Jochem de Neve.

By the 1650s Rembrandt's finances had collapsed and he was renting a house on the Rozengracht. The commission mattered, and the painting hung in the guild's own hall, the Staalhof, until 1771. For a long time the man on the right was thought to be holding a bag of stamps; the 1991 restoration established that it is a pair of gloves.

kids: Everyone here has a hat except one man. Can you spot him, and guess why?

look.text: The open sample book on the table — the thing they have all been interrupted in the middle of.
The servant, bare-headed behind the others, who is not one of the six paying sitters.
The Persian rug over the table, which takes up most of the lower painting — and carries the signature.

timeline.text: Five cloth inspectors and their servant look up from the books, as though somebody had just opened the door — which is to say, as though you had. Rembrandt painted it in 1662, long after the Amsterdam élite had stopped queueing at his studio, and it is the last great group portrait he made.

title.en: The Sampling Officials of the Amsterdam Drapers’ Guild, Known as ‘The Syndics’
title.nl: De waardijns van het Amsterdamse lakenbereidersgilde, bekend als ‘De Staalmeesters’
